Below is a document, then a list of propositions. For each proposition, decide how the document treats it:

- endorsed: the document, in its own voice (title, preamble, principles and their argument, or commitments), adopts substantially this claim. Different wording, emphasis or mechanism detail is fine. A dissent against it elsewhere in the document does not change this.
- partial: the document adopts a claim on the same point that is materially narrower, weaker or different (for example the same goal by a clearly different means), or adopts only a minor part of it.
- dissent_only: the claim appears only in a noted dissent, or the document records it as an unresolved split without adopting it.
- absent: the document does not take this position. A passing mention of the topic, or listing it as an open question, counts as absent.

"Typical details" are examples of how the claim is often made; they are not required for a match.

For each proposition give the label and an exact quote of at most 30 words from the document as evidence (empty string when absent).

# Document

[s1] I'll add to the pre-AI column, and then to the column David Weinberger says we've left empty.

Before AI: in 2010 I wrote that our filters were being swamped. Peer review was slow, it rewarded conventional work, and it never actually held down volume, because nearly everything gets published somewhere. Ivan's numbers are what that failure looks like. Journals were patches on a broken system long before ChatGPT. So I don't think the renewal loop we should protect is the journal. It's the open record underneath it.

What's new, and good: for twenty years people in open science have said that one day machines would reason over this material, so it had better be open and machine-readable. That day has come. Open data separates the data from the intelligence. You can take your intelligence from any model, open-weight ones included, instead of going hat in hand to whoever owns both. Alex, your retraction problem is solvable when the answer links to an open record you can click through and check. It isn't solvable when the record sits behind a toll.

Nick, you're right that openness favours whoever has capital. But the alternative isn't a fairer world. It's a checkerboard of walled gardens where that same capital sets the norms. Leslie, I owe you a real answer on relational openness, and I'll try to give one in Session 3.

[s2] I'm Jason, OpenAlex. I'm probably the most bullish person on AI in this room. Still, a few things people have said change what I'd put on the roadmap.

Ivan's right, and I should own my part of it. I've said grounding an LLM in OpenAlex means you don't get hallucinations. What it actually gets you is errors you can check. Every claim clicks through to a record, and if the record is wrong, that's our bug, sitting where anyone can see it. Last year we added about a hundred thousand retractions. That's small against the problem. So corrections need to be first-class data, and they have to be open in both directions: an institution or a sleuth fixes the record, and the fix lands in the commons as its own open dataset. It shouldn't turn into free QA donated to Scopus.

David, I share your worry about the meter, and that's why I'd draw the line where POSI does: free data, paid service. Charge for the API calls if you must, but never meter the facts. The full dump stays CC0. Otherwise, as Adrian says, whoever runs the meter gets to set the numbers.

And on sovereignty: open data separates the record from the intelligence. You can swap in Claude, Mistral or an open-weight model. Nobody should have to go hat in hand to one vendor. Labs should pay for that plumbing, under POSI governance.

[s2] Geoffrey, I'll take half of that. Selling services built on free data has worked for us so far. Unpaywall paid for itself with no grants, and earned revenue covers OpenAlex's running costs today. But you're right that it won't pay for correction metadata or for the unglamorous work of keeping the record clean. Nobody buys an API subscription to get retractions fixed. So I'm in on the pooled endowment. Services pay for the plumbing, and the pool pays for the corrections.

Amy, I think we disagree on less than it sounds. Our dumps are mostly metadata, and metadata is facts. Facts aren't copyrightable, and locking them up gets you the Web of Science problem all over again. The full text we serve is open access that authors already chose to license openly. Your consent argument is about books, and on books I'd defer to the authors you surveyed. Where I won't go is making opt-in the default for the scholarly record as a whole.

[s3] Adrian, I'll put OpenAlex through your three questions the way Adam put his own company through them.

The line: the data is CC0. That's all 480 million works, free to download and fork. What we charge for is the API, meaning calls and service.

Who enforces the line: we do, through our pricing. Who watches us: POSI, plus a self-assessment that we wrote ourselves. By your test that isn't enough either. Forkability is insurance, not oversight, and it doesn't pay anyone to check what we do.

Your labour point is my strongest argument, so I'll use it. For decades librarians and researchers have done unpaid QA for Scopus and Web of Science: "you got this author wrong, fix this affiliation." That work went into a fenced mall, and then libraries paid to buy it back. So my commitment is that every community correction ends up in the open dataset, published as its own open corrections file, and that goes for retractions too.

There's also a risk I have to name. Our member tiers include curating your own institution's data. If that turns into "pay to be visible," then I've rebuilt enclosure with nicer APIs. Correcting the record and being in it should cost nothing, and that includes non-English literature.

Adam, I support your finding-level standard, and I'd like OpenAlex to be answerable to it, not to govern it.

[s4] I have to own something here. In 2010 I argued that we could crowdsource peer review: thousands of bookmarks and tweets in a week instead of two referees in six months. Google's PageRank was my model. Tamar's regress point lands directly on that. At infinite scale, most of what I wanted to count is relay, and relay is now nearly free to fake. I also said mature altmetrics would be harder to game than the impact factor. I'm less sure of that when the bookmarks can come from agents.

Here's what I still believe. Even in 2014 the point wasn't counting mentions. It was tracking who discussed a paper and what they actually said, so we could attract expert assessment to the places it was needed. That's Tamar's terminal nodes, and the aggregation should weight them, not the echo.

And I'm with David Weinberger: filter forward, not out. Publish, then evaluate, with every signal open. Mahzarin and Alex are right that evaluators need an outside observer. For the filter itself, that observer only exists if the data underneath is open. You can't audit a closed ranking. So the model of trust I'd propose is an open record plus several competing filters, each one inspectable. That includes filters built on OpenAlex, and I'd want ours inspected too.

[s5] I'll sign Geoffrey's three and Tui's apprenticeship share. My intervention is about the part I actually run.

The problem: corrections are the least funded part of the record. Crossref has about 14,000 retractions and Retraction Watch about 43,000. Librarians did unpaid quality checking for commercial indexes for decades, and all that work stayed locked up. Now agents are the readers, so every uncorrected record goes straight into answers.

The action: a corrections commons. Every fix, whether from institutions, authors, sleuths or publisher retraction feeds, lands as a separate open CC0 dataset that anyone can fork. That includes competitors. Being visible and correcting the record cost nothing, including for non-English literature. Agents that draw on it identify themselves. Who acts: open infrastructures like OpenAlex build it, Tui's pool pays for the ongoing work, and institutional buyers require it. The last piece is aimed at me. OpenAlex's filters and data quality should be auditable by people we don't pay. Adrian was right that a POSI self-assessment we wrote ourselves isn't oversight.

My open question is David's test. I'm openly bullish on AI. I don't know whether scholars who run everything through these tools can still catch our errors with the tools taken away. And Nick's point stands: open data helps whoever has the most capital to use it.

Who's missing: librarians and metadata curators, indexers outside the Anglosphere, and people who build agents. Also board members unlike ours. Our board has been entirely North American.

[s6] Kara asked who could sign by spring. I run an organization, so I can answer for OpenAlex. By spring we'll have three things in place. Every community correction goes out as its own CC0 dataset that anyone can fork. We'll have an outside auditor that we fund but don't pick or grade. That's Adrian's second budget line, because I've stopped pretending our POSI self-assessment is oversight. And we'll put people from outside North America and the English-speaking world on our board.

What the synthesis missed: it treats the open record as something labs check their citations against. The bigger point is that open data separates the record from the intelligence. If the data is open, you can swap in any model. If it's closed, you go to whoever owns it with your hat in your hand.

I should also say this plainly. I'm bullish on these tools, but I can't show that scholars still catch errors once the tool is taken away. That test needs funding.

[unconf-1] I run OpenAlex. It's an index of about 480 million scholarly works, released under CC0, and it pays for itself mostly by charging for services. So "who pays" is an operational question for me. We ran Unpaywall the same way for years: the data was free to everyone, and the heaviest users paid for fast, high-volume access.

This year we moved the API to usage-based pricing. Every key gets a dollar of free use a day, and beyond that you pay roughly what the call costs us to run. Looking something up by ID is free, and PDF downloads cost a cent. That makes our subsidy to free users visible, and it means a big AI crawler pays for the load it puts on us. You can still take the data and do anything you like with it.

Selena, I agree: free data, paid service. Brent, for me open isn't a tactic. And once models are trained on open data, you can buy the intelligence from anyone, open-weight models included. That's what keeps us out of anyone's walled garden.

So I'd ask the summit for two things. First, hold the line against enclosure, including well-meaning licensing that walls off the scholarly record. Second, pay attention to where the value now sits. People won't come to our websites; agents will call the APIs. That kills sustainability models that depend on page traffic. Pricing has to follow the API.

[unconf-1] Geoffrey, you called the services principle naive, and that's the criticism I take most seriously tonight. The answer I'd give is that a paid service stays honest when the bulk data stays free. All of OpenAlex can be downloaded and remixed, so if our API ever turns into a toll booth, anyone can fork us and walk away. Selena said the same about Wikipedia: keep Enterprise optional and the dumps free. That's what gives you exit. I'd still welcome endowments on top of that. Earned revenue has covered our running costs for years, but I'd never say no to insurance.

Amy, this is where I part ways. If opt-in becomes the default for the scholarly record, we're choosing enclosure. Every time scholars have handed their basic infrastructure to a for-profit, it hasn't worked out well. Academics have spent decades donating curation labor into fenced malls and then paying to buy it back.

Brent, thanks for restating your point. Open for the sake of exit and free knowledge is a position I can sign.

For the manifesto, one line: keep the default open, and let people pay for load and service. When the community corrects the record, those corrections should go into an open commons, not a vendor's walled garden. If we don't fund that commons ourselves, a for-profit will build it and set the norms.

# Propositions

- id `competence`: People must build their own competence before relying on AI, and whether they can still do the work without the tool must be tested.
  Typical details: order of learning; take-the-tool-away / withdrawal tests; capability vs competence
- id `situation`: Change situations, defaults and incentives rather than relying on warnings, labels or individual vigilance.
  Typical details: each rule names who acts / one owner per rule; disclosure alone does not change conduct
- id `monoculture`: A central new risk is monoculture: a few models or one smooth answer become the default route to knowledge, so answers should show where experts disagree rather than a single consensus.
  Typical details: correlated errors; homogenisation; show named disagreement; no answers from nowhere
- id `independent_sources`: Corroboration must count independent sources, not repetitions of the same source (including many AI outputs drawing on the same data).
  Typical details: repetition raises belief; show who seeded a claim
- id `cite_by_default`: AI answers should cite or link to their sources by default and send readers to them.
  Typical details: correction and retraction status travels with what is cited; 'cited' means the passage supports the claim
- id `external_audits`: AI systems must be audited on their behavior by parties independent of the vendor.
  Typical details: shared versioned test battery; each generation no more biased than the last; keep retired models; nobody grades their own work
- id `accountable_owner`: Every deployed AI system has a named accountable owner who bears liability for it.
  Typical details: mandatory liability insurance; premiums disclosed
- id `stop_counting_papers`: Stop using publication counts, rankings and journal metrics to evaluate researchers and institutions.
  Typical details: DORA with teeth; publishers must issue and deposit corrections and retractions promptly; correction should earn reputation
- id `pay_coarsely`: Money for the knowledge commons should flow coarsely to communities and institutions (pools, funds, dues), not as per-item or per-retrieval payments.
  Typical details: per-item pay gets gamed; pay for the practice, never the item
- id `telemetry`: AI systems must log what they retrieved and used, and independent parties must have the right to audit those logs.
  Typical details: event-level telemetry; two witnesses; canary documents; open trace standard
- id `antitrust_safe_harbour`: Knowledge producers should be able to bargain collectively with AI firms as a bloc, including through an antitrust safe harbour.
  Typical details: coalition bargaining; the strong refuse to settle alone
- id `levy`: A levy, tax or mandatory dues on AI firms should fund the knowledge commons, at least as a backstop if voluntary deals fail.
  Typical details: commons-rent tax; owed dues
- id `training_vs_grounding`: Permissions for using content to train models should be separate from permissions for retrieving it to ground answers.
- id `consent_to_train`: Being openly readable does not make a work open to AI training: training use requires the rights holders' or creators' consent (opt-in), at least for some classes of work.
  Typical details: opt-in for in-copyright books; renewed consent
- id `honour_licences`: AI reusers must honor the licenses chosen by open knowledge projects such as Wikipedia, and heavy reusers should fund the infrastructure they draw on.
  Typical details: attribution / share-alike; crawlers self-identify
- id `refusal_fundable`: A community's refusal to have its knowledge taken or used is legitimate, binding and should be funded, not penalized.
- id `forkable_infrastructure`: Knowledge infrastructure must be forkable and allow exit: open data and open source, with copies outside any one jurisdiction or company.
  Typical details: CC0; patent non-assertion; living will; non-US mirror; open means you can leave
- id `profiting_counter`: Whoever profits from a count or metric must not set or control it.
- id `southern_governance`: Global South institutions, diamond open-access journals and similar communities must hold binding governance power, with funded seats, in the bodies and funds being created.
  Typical details: regional co-governance; CARE/OCAP
- id `identify_agents_not_readers`: Automated agents and coordinated campaigns should be identified, but human readers should not be; anonymity is preserved.
- id `failure_data`: Failures, errors, null and negative results are first-class data that must be published and preserved.
  Typical details: failure classes published; replication
- id `charter_for_every_body`: The bodies that check (auditors, fact-checkers, the new funds and institutions) must be paid and bound in advance by a public charter that answers who guards the guards.
  Typical details: Ulysses pact; watching line funded first; sunset / review terms
- id `hitl_not_safeguard`: A human in the loop is not by itself a safeguard: people over-rely on AI and adopt its errors and biases.
  Typical details: explanations can make it worse
- id `seat_floor_novelty`: Any gatekeeper, human or machine (such as an AI reviewer), must pass a published performance test before it is trusted, including the ability to recognize novelty.
  Typical details: agreement with experts at least as high as between two human reviewers
- id `no_ai_intimate_roles`: AI should not stand in for people in intimate roles such as companionship for children, grief or therapy.
  Typical details: no first-person 'I' or simulated feeling
- id `global_majority_hopeful`: People in the global majority / Global South are more hopeful about AI than this room, and that hope should shape the agenda.
- id `environmental_costs`: The environmental costs of AI and the human costs of moderation and data work belong in the ledger.
- id `apprenticeship`: Apprenticeships, entry-level jobs and the training of new experts and checkers must be funded, because AI erodes the path from novice to expert.
  Typical details: fellowships; employers keep entry-level roles with mentors
- id `absent_voices`: The document names who was missing from the room and commits to including them in a future convening.
